criteria.note: Water shut-off ball valves are visible in the open access panel, next to filters and water meters.
Red lever handles and small white lever handles are clearly visible.
No drips, water, corrosion or stains are visible on the valves or fittings.

rows.note: Flat's tiled access hatch: two red-lever ball valves, filters and water meters, no visible leak or stains. Lever position must not be judged.

criteria.note: A blue ball valve is visible on the pipe just below the water meter.
The blue lever handle of the ball valve is clearly in frame.
I can't see any water, drips, stains or corrosion on the valve or its brass fittings.

rows.note: Outdoor meter with a blue-lever ball valve below; the valve is partly cut off at the bottom edge, so a retake is defensible.

criteria.note: The photo shows a loose electronic water meter on a table, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible.
No valve is shown, so leaks at the valve can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed main water shut-off valve, with its handle and the pipe joints around it in frame.
rows.note: Electronic water meter lying on a table, not installed; no shut-off valve in frame.

criteria.note: An outdoor manifold with several water meters and shut-off valves is visible; which one serves the flat is unclear.
Valve handles are visible, e.g. near the top meter and beside the lower meters.
The pipes look discoloured, but the black-and-white photo makes corrosion or stains hard to confirm.

rows.retakeHint: Take a close, well-lit colour photo of your flat's own shut-off valve so its condition can be checked.
rows.note: Black-and-white outdoor wall with several meters and small valves of a shared building; which valve is the home's is unclear and corrosion can't be judged in B/W. Corroded pipework makes fix_first defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: This photo shows a water meter, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible in the frame.
Can't judge because the valve isn't in the photo.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve next to the meter, with its handle in the frame.
rows.note: Close-up of a dirty meter dial, no valve in frame (sample photo).

criteria.note: Photo shows an outdoor meter box and pipe fittings in a street excavation, not the flat's shut-off valve.
No shut-off valve handle or lever is visible.
The flat's valve isn't in the photo, so its condition can't be checked.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the main water shut-off valve inside your flat, usually under the kitchen sink, with its handle in view.
rows.note: Street excavation with the utility's meter box, lid closed, no lever visible; wrong subject (the valve is inside the building).

criteria.note: A brass ball shut-off valve on a copper water pipe is clearly visible.
The metal lever with a green grip is fully in frame.
No drips, water, stains or corrosion visible; only normal brass patina and solder marks.

rows.note: Brass ball valve with a green lever on copper pipe, clean (sample photo).

criteria.note: A brass ball-type shut-off valve on copper pipework is clearly in frame.
The dark green lever handle is fully visible.
No drips, water or clear corrosion are visible at the valve. Solder joints look dry.

rows.note: Brass ball valve on copper pipe with a black lever; the lever position is ambiguous but never judged.

criteria.note: Close-up of a loose braided hose section only; no tap or machine connection in frame.
No shut-off tap is visible in the photo.
Visible braid looks intact, but connections and full hose length are not shown.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the whole hose from the wall tap to the back of the washing machine.
rows.note: Macro of a braided steel hose only: neither the machine nor its tap is in frame.

criteria.note: A braided hose rises to a cut-off fitting, apparently under a basin; no washing machine is visible.
A chrome angle valve is partly visible and blurred; unclear if it serves the washing machine.
The visible braided section looks intact, but the full hose and machine connection are not shown.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the washing machine's tap and the whole fill hose up to the machine, in focus.
rows.note: Braided hose into a chrome angle valve, shallow focus; no machine in frame, so the hose is not visible from tap to machine.

criteria.note: A white plastic sink trap (P-trap) is clearly visible.
Water is actively dripping from the bottom of the trap bend.

rows.fix: Clean the drain or trap: lift the cover, remove hair and dirt, and rinse. Tighten a leaking nut.
rows.note: White plastic sink trap with water dripping from it: leak at the trap, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: Photo shows a loose brass valve fitting with thread tape, not an installed dishwasher connection.
The valve is a loose part, so no installed dishwasher shut-off tap is shown.
No installed hose or connection is shown, so leaks can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed dishwasher hose and its shut-off tap under the sink, with good lighting.
rows.note: A hand holding a loose brass valve with thread tape: a loose part, not an installed connection. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: White plastic sink trap and waste pipes are clearly visible under the sink.
No drips, water stains or standing water visible on the trap, joints or cabinet floor.

rows.note: Open under-sink cupboard: plastic trap with an appliance branch, dry clean floor, no leak. (No drip tray, but that is L4, not L5.)

criteria.note: Only a small part of a white pipe shows under the sink; the trap itself is hidden.
The trap area is blocked from view, so leaks or water can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: With the cabinet clear, photograph the sink trap straight on with good lighting.
rows.note: A person lying in an open sink cupboard (legs only); the trap is not clearly visible. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Only the sink basin drain holes show; the trap is hidden behind closed cabinet doors.
Basins look dry, but the trap can't be seen to check for leaks or blockage.

rows.retakeHint: Open the cabinet doors under the sink and photograph the trap and pipes with good lighting.
rows.note: Kitchen with the lower cupboard doors closed; the trap is not visible (sample photo).

criteria.note: This shows a toilet tank supply hose and angle valve, not a dishwasher connection.
The visible shut-off tap serves the toilet, not a dishwasher.
Dishwasher hose not shown; no water or stains visible on this toilet fitting.

rows.retakeHint: Open the sink cabinet and photograph the dishwasher inlet hose where it connects to its shut-off tap.
rows.note: Toilet supply: braided hose and angle stop valve under a toilet cistern; wrong appliance for the dishwasher check.

criteria.note: A distribution board with rows of circuit breakers is clearly visible.
Covers and blanking plates are in place; no scorch marks or exposed parts seen.
Several RCDs with TEST buttons are visible on the left of each row.
Nothing is stored in front of the board in the visible area.

rows.note: Modern ABB board: RCDs with TEST buttons, B16 breakers, labelled circuits, cover on (sample photo).

criteria.note: An old meter board with screw-in fuse holders is visible.
Fuse holder covers are removed, terminals and wiring are exposed, and the wall has dark soot marks.
I can't see an RCD with a TEST button on this board.
Tools, removed covers and parts are lying directly in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old single-phase installation with porcelain screw-fuse holders, a removed fuse and tools on the floor: exposed parts, no RCD.

criteria.note: This looks like a new, empty, uninstalled board enclosure with its cover off, not an installed fuse box.
Can't judge an installed board from a product photo of an empty enclosure.
No breakers or RCD are fitted in this empty enclosure.
The board isn't installed, so I can't see what's stored around it.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph your home's installed fuse box from the front with its cover on, so the breakers and any TEST button show.
rows.note: An empty consumer-unit enclosure with its cover beside it, bare DIN rail, no breakers: not an installed board. fix_first (missing cover, no RCD) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A distribution board with breakers and RCBOs is clearly in frame.
The front cover is missing, so wiring, terminals and the busbar are exposed.
RCBO and RC devices with test buttons are visible.
Nothing is stored in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Consumer unit with its front cover removed: RCBOs and exposed terminals, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: Wall-mounted breaker panel is clearly in frame with the door open.
The cover is in place and the blank slots are closed, with no scorch marks or damage visible.
Breakers 6 and 12 have yellow TEST buttons.
Nothing is stored against or in front of the panel.

rows.note: US breaker panel, door open, dead front on, handwritten circuit numbers, two GFCI breakers with TEST buttons (residual-current protection).

criteria.note: This is a product photo of a single loose RCD module, not an installed fuse box.
Can't judge the installed board's condition from a product photo.
An RCD with a TEST button is shown, but it isn't installed in a board.
The board's surroundings aren't shown.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph your own installed fuse box with the cover closed, showing the whole board and the area in front of it.
rows.note: Product photo of an ABB RCD on a white background: not the home's board.

criteria.note: An old wall-mounted distribution board with many metal enclosures is clearly visible.
Covers look in place, but there is rust on the backing plate and chipped, corroded enclosures.
No device with a TEST button is visible; there are only closed enclosures and old rotary switches.
A coiled cable with a plug is hanging in front of the dark brown enclosure.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old industrial cast-metal switchgear (ASEA) with covers on but no RCD visible. A retake (not a home board) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: An open metal distribution board with a meter, fuses and terminals is clearly visible.
Loose connections sit outside the enclosure on top, and bare terminals are exposed inside without an inner cover.
There's a small modular device beside the meter, but no TEST button can be seen.
Nothing is stored in front of the board.

rows.retakeHint: Take a close-up of the modular devices beside the meter so any TEST button can be seen.
rows.note: Open metal cabinet in an outbuilding: meter, screw fuses, main switch and exposed empty fuse bases; RCD not clearly visible.
